definition: Sticking rigidly to a theory or set of rules without caring whether it works in practice.
example: Her doctrinaire approach to healthy eating left no room for even one slice of birthday cake.
nuance: Doctrinaire stresses applying a theory no matter the practical results; dogmatic stresses stating opinions as if beyond question.
prompt: A youth soccer coach follows a single tactical theory no matter who the team plays.
options: The doctrinaire coach kept the same formation even when it was plainly losing matches.
The doctrinaire coach changed tactics every week after carefully studying each new opponent's habits.
The doctrinaire coach bandaged a sprained ankle on the sidelines.
The doctrinaire coach had earned an advanced degree in sports science.
reasons: Clinging to a theory despite clear evidence that it fails is exactly this kind of rigidity.
Adapting to each situation is flexible and practical, the reverse of rigid adherence.
This mistakes the word for something medical; it describes rigid thinking, not doctoring.
Holding a degree shows expertise, not stubborn devotion to one theory.

practice.prompt: A baker follows a century-old bread method from an inherited notebook.
options: The doctrinaire baker taught a lively class to children at the library.
The doctrinaire baker sold her loaves at the farmers' market every Saturday.
Though every loaf came out dense, the doctrinaire baker refused to alter one step of the method.
The doctrinaire baker cheerfully swapped in whatever flour was in the pantry and adjusted the water by feel.
reasons: This confuses the word with teaching; it means rigid devotion to a theory, not instruction.
A regular selling schedule says nothing about an unbending attachment to theory.
Refusing to adjust a method after repeated failure shows impractical loyalty to rules.
Improvising based on results is flexible, not rigidly rule-bound.
